cards.headline: Linear perspective
lines: Parallel lines appear to meet at a vanishing point on the horizon.
Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated the method in Florence in the early 1400s.
It let Renaissance painters create convincing depth on a flat surface.
cards.source: Gombrich, 'The Story of Art'; Edgerton, 'The Renaissance Rediscovery of Linear Perspective' (1975).

cards.headline: Complementary colours
lines: Colours opposite each other on the colour wheel — like blue and orange — are complementary.
Side by side, they make each other look more intense.
Painters and designers use them to make a subject pop.
cards.source: Chevreul, 'The Principles of Harmony and Contrast of Colours' (1839); Itten, 'The Art of Color' (1961).

cards.headline: Why an octave sounds like the same note
lines: Going up an octave doubles a note's frequency.
Concert A is 440 Hz; the A above it is 880 Hz.
Because the waves line up so neatly, the two notes blend almost as one.
cards.source: ISO 16 (standard tuning A = 440 Hz); Rossing, 'The Science of Sound'.

cards.headline: Time signatures count the beat
lines: A time signature tells you how many beats are in each bar.
4/4 has four beats — most pop music uses it.
3/4 has three: the ONE-two-three of a waltz.
cards.source: Taylor, 'The AB Guide to Music Theory', Part I.

cards.headline: The rule of thirds
lines: Imagine the frame split into a 3 × 3 grid.
Placing the subject on a line or crossing, rather than dead centre, often feels more dynamic.
It's a guideline — centred compositions can be powerful too.
cards.source: Smith, 'Remarks on Rural Scenery' (1797), which named it; standard photography texts.

cards.question: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
cards.why: Leonardo, in the early 1500s. It hangs in the Louvre in Paris.
cards.source: Musée du Louvre, collection record; Kemp, 'Leonardo da Vinci: The Marvellous Works of Nature and Man'.

cards.question: In traditional painting, the three primary colours are…
cards.why: Painters traditionally mix from red, yellow and blue. Screens use red, green and blue light; printers use cyan, magenta and yellow.
cards.source: Itten, 'The Art of Color'; Gage, 'Colour and Culture'.

cards.question: Beethoven composed his Ninth Symphony while he was…
cards.why: His hearing declined from his late twenties; by the Ninth (1824) he was almost totally deaf.

cards.question: A note vibrates at 440 Hz. The same note one octave higher vibrates at…
cards.why: An octave up doubles the frequency: 440 × 2 = 880.

cards.question: Impressionism takes its name from a painting by…
cards.why: Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise' (1872). A critic used the title to mock the group — and the name stuck.
cards.source: Gombrich, 'The Story of Art'; Musée Marmottan Monet.

cards.headline: The Starry Night was painted at an asylum
cards.text: Van Gogh made it in 1889 at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, drawing on the view from his window. He sold very few paintings in his lifetime.
cards.source: Museum of Modern Art, New York, collection record; Naifeh & Smith, 'Van Gogh: The Life' (2011).

cards.headline: Ultramarine blue once rivalled gold in price
cards.text: Ground from lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan, it was so costly that Renaissance contracts sometimes specified it for the Virgin Mary's robes.
cards.source: Ball, 'Bright Earth: The Invention of Colour' (2001).

cards.headline: A standard piano has 88 keys
cards.text: 52 white and 36 black, spanning just over seven octaves.
cards.source: Standard modern piano specification; Rossing, 'The Science of Sound'.

cards.headline: Some cave art is over 40,000 years old
cards.text: Paintings in Sulawesi, Indonesia, have been dated to more than 40,000 years ago — made with ochre pigments.
cards.source: Aubert et al. (2014), Nature; Brumm et al. (2021), Science Advances.

cards.headline: How chords work

steps.headline: 1 · Twelve steps
lines: Western music divides the octave into 12 semitones.
On a piano, each key — white or black — is one semitone from the next.

steps.headline: 2 · The major chord
lines: Stack a root, the note 4 semitones up, and the note 7 up: C–E–G.
Major chords tend to sound bright.

steps.headline: 3 · The minor chord
lines: Lower the middle note by one semitone: C–E♭–G.
Minor chords tend to sound darker.

steps.headline: 4 · Progressions
lines: Many songs cycle through a few chords, such as I–V–vi–IV.
In C major, that's C, G, A minor, F.

cards.source: Taylor, 'The AB Guide to Music Theory'; Levine, 'The Jazz Theory Book'.

cards.headline: Art & music: the takeaways
points: Parallel lines meet at a vanishing point.
Complementary colours sit opposite on the wheel.
A time signature counts the beats in a bar.
Off-centre subjects can feel more dynamic.
